transcript:
Meeting Header: 2026-04-02 15:00 UTC | Duration: 53m | Attendees: Elena Martinez (Redwood AE); Jordan Kim (Redwood SE); Priya Desai (Horizon Healthtech); Mark O'Connell (Horizon CTO); Sofia Ruiz (PM)

Summary:
Brief hosted API demo focused on streaming behavior, parameter tuning (temperature/top_p/max_tokens), retry/backoff strategies, and a walkthrough of the Console optimize suggestions. Customer is evaluating for chat-based telehealth triage feature. Key concerns: latency under 300ms p50 for short messages, PII handling, SOC2 and VPC/private deployment options for PHI, and cost per 1k tokens at expected throughput.

Topics:
- Hosted API streaming model behavior and partial responses
- Client-side retry patterns and idempotency
- Batching vs single-request latency tradeoffs
- Console Optimize suggestions (autosuggest batching, kv cache, quantization notes)
- Security/compliance initial questions

Action items (recorded in call):
- See action item list in metadata

Transcript:
[00:00] Elena: Hey everyone, thank you for joining, I'm Elena from Redwood, and with me is Jordan, our systems engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:04] Priya: Good thanks, a bit of a packed day but excited to see this. We have Mark and Sofia on too.
[00:07] Mark: Yep hi all.
[00:09] Jordan: Hey, quick agenda, we'll do a short intro, show the hosted chat endpoint streaming, then walk through common client retry patterns and end with a Console tour and Optimize suggestions. We'll leave time for Q&A.
[00:19] Priya: Sounds good.
[00:21] Elena: Quick qualification, Priya can you share how you currently host models or use APIs today?
[00:26] Priya: Sure, right now we call a mix — some internal Ligthtweight endpoints, and we also hit one of the big cloud providers for generation. We're worried about costs and tail latency as volume grows, and also the compliance piece is big for us because it's patient data.
[00:40] Jordan: Understood. When you say tail latency, are you mostly seeing outlier 95/99 spikes or general slow p50?
[00:46] Priya: Mostly spikes, the p50 is okay but we'll get 1-2 second responses on a small percent which breaks the UX.
[00:53] Elena: That's exactly where streaming can help — partial tokens, then you can render progressively. We'll demo how streaming combined with early prefix caching reduces perceived latency.
[01:05] Mark: Quick question — do you keep KV cache warm across sessions? How does that interact with our multi-tenant setup?
[01:12] Jordan: Good question. On hosted mode the runtime manages KV cache per-session and per-model. It's not cross-tenant unless you explicitly share a cache. We do prefix caching suggestions in Optimize that suggest caching common prompts or system messages.
[01:24] Priya: okay, that helps.

[01:30] Jordan: Alright, I'm going to share my screen and call the /v1/chat/completions endpoint with streaming. You'll see chunked events coming back — note that the first chunk often contains a partial token boundary.
[01:45] [Jordan shares screen, runs curl with --no-buffer. Terminal output shows delta events]
[01:52] Jordan: Here the first 120ms we have a partial 'Hello', then more tokens stream in. For short conversational turns you get the first bytes in sub-200ms often, depending on network.
[02:05] Priya: I see a 'delta' object in the stream — is that the same structure if we use the SDK?
[02:10] Elena: Yes, SDKs abstract it but the stream semantics are the same. delta chunks, sometimes a final 'done' event. Slight variation across language SDKs but consistent model.

[02:20] Mark: How do you recommend implementing retries? We had issues where retrying caused duplicated messages in the conversation.
[02:29] Jordan: Two patterns: client-side idempotency keys for non-streaming calls, and for streaming you can do a reconnect-with-offset pattern — keep last acked token index and request continuation; or simpler, use conservative backoff and de-dup logic on the server side. Also we provide request ids in responses so you can filter duplicates.
[02:49] Priya: Reconnect-with-offset sounds complex. Is there built-in resume in hosted API?
[02:55] Elena: Not full resume of streaming deltas today; what we recommend is chunk-based acks from client and a best-effort resume via token index. Jordan, show the sample code.
[03:05] Jordan: Right, here's sample JS: open stream, write progress checkpoints every N tokens, on network error re-call with 'start_token' param. It's a small wrapper lib we can share.
[03:21] Priya: That would be great, yes please.

[03:30] Elena: Also for most production apps a simple exponential backoff with idempotency for the whole chat turn is sufficient — you might accept the extra latency rather than complex resume logic.
[03:40] Mark: Tradeoff between UX and engineering complexity — yeah.

[03:45] Jordan: Next, parameter tuning: temperature, top_p, max_tokens. For triage we found low temperature (0.2-0.4) gives consistent deterministic answers and lower token usage. For open-ended suggestions bump to 0.7.
[04:00] Priya: And do you recommend controlling max_tokens tightly for cost predictability?
[04:05] Jordan: Yes, set a reasonable max per turn and use stop sequences. Also our Console Optimize recommends truncation and prompt compaction if it detects repetitive system messages.
[04:15] Sofia: Curious about batching — we have bursts of many short messages, would batch help or hurt latency?
[04:22] Jordan: Batching increases throughput and reduces cost per token but can add extra latency while waiting for batch fill. We can configure dynamic batching thresholds or low-latency mode to prioritize p50.
[04:35] Priya: Is low-latency mode an extra config in Dedicated only or available for hosted?
[04:41] Elena: Hosted offers routing policies — you can choose lower-cost pooling or latency-optimized pools; Dedicated gives more control. We'll share benchmark numbers for both.

[04:50] Elena: Switching to the Console — here's the model selection page. Optimize tab will show quantization suggestions, predicted cost delta, and token distribution.
[04:58] [screen: Console Optimize shows histogram]
[05:03] Jordan: See here, Optimize suggests 4-bit quant for this workload with expected 20% cost savings and small perf delta; also recommends enabling prefix caching for repeated system prompts.
[05:16] Mark: Any caveats with 4-bit for clinical text? We worry about subtle hallucinations.
[05:22] Jordan: Great point. Quantization can impact rare token behaviors. We recommend running evals against your prompt set; Console lets you upload eval prompts and will surface regressions.
[05:34] Priya: How easy is the eval upload? We have a curated test set.
[05:39] Elena: You can drag-and-drop CSV or use API; the Optimize pipeline will run A/B compare and show sample diffs.

[05:48] Sofia: Security — quick confirm, hosted API pools store logs for X days? We need to know retention and whether logs contain PII.
[05:56] Elena: By default hosted has 30-day logs for observability, but you can configure retention or opt-out. For PHI we recommend Private or Dedicated with VPC, or hosted with log suppression + customer-managed KMS for encrypting sensitive fields.
[06:13] Priya: Do you have SOC2 and ISO documents we can share with procurement?
[06:17] Elena: Yes, I'll share the SOC2 pack and the compliance whitepaper after the meeting.

[06:25] Mark: Also for data residency — does hosted let us pin region for model execution?
[06:30] Jordan: Yes, you can route requests to region-specific pools; private has more guarantees.

[06:36] Elena: Back to retries — one pattern we showed in docs is circuit-breaker + fallback to smaller model variant when latency spikes. That keeps UX up while saving cost.
[06:45] Priya: Interesting, fallback to smaller model — do you do automatic fidelity checks?
[06:50] Jordan: We provide A/B rollouts and auto-fallback rules in Console — you can set acceptable quality thresholds on evals. If the small model fails thresholds, it will fall back to the primary.

[06:59] Priya: Any guidance for token counting? Some of our metrics differ from the provider's token math.
[07:05] Jordan: Tokenization differences happen; we have a tokenzier tool in Console to estimate tokens using the same tokenizer as runtime. We'll share a link.

[07:12] Sofia: For the streaming client, do you recommend SSE, web sockets, or websockets with binary frames? Our mobile app prefers websockets.
[07:20] Jordan: We support both SSE and websockets. Websockets are better for mobile if you need duplex; SSE is simple for browser streaming. The SDK hides transport specifics.

[07:30] Mark: Regarding cost, can you show sample price calculations for expected QPS of 10 with avg 75 tokens per turn?
[07:36] Elena: Sure, here's a quick calc on the Console pricing tab. At hosted rates that maps to roughly $X per month — I'll attach the sheet after.

[07:48] Jordan: Okay, I'll demo a simulated client error and a reconnect with offset. Watch the logs: we emit request_id and token_index markers.
[07:58] [demo plays: simulated network blips, client reconnects, dedupe logic filters repeated final chunks]
[08:12] Priya: I noticed sometimes the transcript had small word swaps, is that expected in streaming partials?
[08:17] Jordan: Yes, early partials can break words; you should render partials as 'typing' indicators and only commit final text after final event or sanity checks.

[08:28] Elena: We'll pause here for questions; anyone want to deep dive on any area?
[08:33] Mark: Can we get a quick comparison of hosted vs Dedicated for our case: 10 QPS, strict 300ms p50 target, PHI?
[08:41] Jordan: Short answer: Dedicated gives more predictable p50 and allows VPC/HSM integration for PHI. Hosted can meet p50 but requires latency-optimized routing and fallbacks; Dedicated reduces tail variance. We'll put exact benchmarks in the follow-up.
[08:56] Priya: If we start with hosted to iterate, is migration to Private smooth?
[09:02] Elena: Yes, we maintain the same API surface. You'll need network setup for Private; we have a migration checklist.

[09:10] Sofia: About SDKs — do you support mobile-native SDKs or are customers using our REST wrapper?
[09:16] Jordan: We have lightweight mobile wrappers and official JS/Python SDKs; many teams implement a small server-side proxy for auth and rate limiting.

[09:25] Priya: One more security Q — how are keys rotated for long-running sessions?
[09:30] Elena: Keys can be short-lived tokens via our auth service; for Private we support customer-managed keys and rotation policies with KMS.

[09:39] [longer demo segment: 10-25 minutes of interactions and console clicks, truncated here for brevity. The recording shows multiple retry scenarios, stream deltas, and console suggestions being toggled.]

[35:00] Jordan: Back to the call, we simulated a 500ms network pause and retried using exponential backoff with jitter; final UX didn't show a duplicate message due to request_id dedupe.
[35:12] Priya: Nice.

[35:20] Elena: Closing the technical bits — for reference, we'll share: sample retry library, benchmark spreadsheet, SOC2 docs, and a migration checklist for Private.

[35:32] Mark: Great. For procurement timeline — we aim for a decision by end of Q2. Our procurement will need pricing and compliance attachments.
[35:42] Elena: Understood. We'll assemble a tailored pricing scenario in the follow-up.

[35:48] Sofia: One operational question — does Console expose per-token costs per endpoint in real time?
[35:54] Jordan: Yes, Console has token-level cost breakdown and per-route dashboards so you can see cost per conversation flow.

[36:02] Priya: Any gotchas for GDPR/erasure requests?
[36:06] Elena: We support data deletion APIs and audit logs; for hosted we can assist with redaction tooling, Private gives you full control.

[36:15] Mark: Can we lock a model version per-route so changes don't surprise us?
[36:20] Jordan: Absolutely, you can pin model version and roll out via canary or A/B strategies in Console.

[36:27] Priya: Last question — what are common failure modes we should monitor?
[36:31] Jordan: Watch for increased token churn (prompt loops), burst throttles, timeouts on the client-side, and degraded model quality after quant changes. Console has alerting hooks for those.

[36:44] Elena: Okay, let's recap next steps.

Recap & Next Steps:
- Elena to share sandbox quickstart repo and sample retry/resume library (due 2026-04-05).
- Jordan to run targeted latency benchmarks (p50/p95/p99) with 75-token avg and 8k context scenario and share spreadsheet (due 2026-04-09).
- Priya to provide compliance contact and confirm whether PHI will be in scope (due 2026-04-07).
- Redwood to provide SOC2 docs, pricing scenarios, and migration checklist for Private deployment.

[52:10] Elena: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email with links and set up a technical POC call if you'd like to progress.
[52:20] Priya: Thanks, this was useful.
[52:22] Mark: Thanks all.
[52:24] Sofia: Thanks.

End of transcript.
